tldr: We propose S-BFM, a control model that enables humanoids to autonomously organize whole-body transitions and movement pace to arrive right on schedule using only sparse goals specifying where, in which posture, and when to arrive, without requiring detailed trajectory instructions.
hero_caption: Overview of the three-stage S-BFM framework. Stage I learns behavior representations embedded with world coordinates, Stage II distills the pacing of real motions conditioned on remaining time from a teacher model, and Stage III augments diverse distance and duration variations using a generative model.
overview:
In conventional whole-body humanoid control, tracking dense reference trajectories at every frame has been the dominant approach. However, real-world task instructions are much more naturally given as sparse spatiotemporal goals (where, in which posture, and when to arrive), such as "go crouch in front of the desk 2 meters away in 3 seconds." Controllers that require dense trajectories force a higher-level planner to continuously generate frame-by-frame intermediate trajectories and transition motions, making adaptation difficult whenever targets change.

The authors drew inspiration from human motor coordination. When humans walk, the cerebral cortex decides on broad destinations, while the cerebellum, brainstem, and spinal cord subconsciously adjust step lengths and whole-body coordination using sensory feedback. Mimicking this mechanism, the core idea of this work asks: can a low-level controller organize the intervening motion and its pace by itself directly from its current physical state, relying solely on sparse goals and remaining time?

The proposed S-BFM uses a behavioral latent space based on Forward-Backward representations and is trained across three stages. First is Spatial Grounding, which learns position and heading in world coordinates. Second is Time-Conditioned Distillation, which learns natural transitions and pacing conditioned on remaining time from a dense teacher. Third is Generative Fine-Tuning, which augments combinations of distances and arrival times not found in real data using a generative model.

In simulator experiments with the Unitree G1, S-BFM reduced global joint-position error by over 32% compared to the best baseline and demonstrated high goal-reaching rates even under disturbances. Furthermore, real-world deployment on the full-size humanoid AGIBOT A3 demonstrated autonomous switching between walking and running depending on specified arrival times, as well as standing up from the floor, proving that sparse spatiotemporal goals suffice for natural, well-timed whole-body motion.
contributions: Formulated a control problem where a low-level controller autonomously generates natural whole-body transition motions and movement pacing from sparse spatiotemporal goals (target posture, world coordinates, and arrival time).
Proposed the three-stage S-BFM framework comprising Spatial Grounding, Time-Conditioned Distillation, and Generative Fine-Tuning.

Significantly outperformed existing whole-body control methods in reaching accuracy and posture-holding performance in simulation, and demonstrated motion generation and deployment from sparse goals on a full-size AGIBOT A3 humanoid.

sections.heading: No More Dense Trajectories? Controlling Humanoids Like a Cerebellum
sections.summary: Recent whole-body trackers can execute diverse motions, but they require dense trajectory instructions at every frame. Inspired by human motor coordination, this paper proposes S-BFM, which autonomously generates intervening motions from sparse goals specifying target posture, pose, and arrival time.
sections.details:
Humanoid robot control has transitioned from task-specific policies to general-purpose whole-body trackers leveraging large-scale motion datasets and physics simulation. However, while these models excel at faithfully tracking given dense trajectories, they cannot create the intervening motions themselves. As a result, whenever a target changes, a separate planner must smoothly interpolate and regenerate a new intermediate trajectory from scratch.

Looking at human movement, however, the cerebral cortex selects rough goals and paths, the brainstem and spinal cord support basic walking patterns, and the cerebellum harmonizes motion using sensory feedback. Humans do not consciously calculate joint angles at every step. From this insight, the authors posed a question: can a low-level controller receive only a target position, target posture, and arrival time, and organize the intervening whole-body motion on its own from its current physical state?

Existing latent-space approaches (such as BFM-Zero, BeJEPA, and PLAT) exist, but none have simultaneously achieved accurate position and heading control in world coordinates, natural whole-body transitions between targets, and proper pacing tailored to a specified arrival time. S-BFM addresses each of these three challenges step-by-step through a three-stage learning approach, achieving autonomous control driven entirely by sparse instructions without using any intermediate reference trajectories.

sections.heading: How S-BFM Differs from Existing Trackers and Latent Space Models
sections.summary: This section reviews three areas: dense-reference whole-body control, goal-conditioned latent representations, and motion in-betweening. S-BFM overcomes their shortcomings, achieving both temporal adaptation and spatial control under physical closed-loop execution.
sections.details:
Related work broadly spans three areas:

- Dense-reference whole-body control:
Imitation learning using physics simulation (such as SONIC, SuperMimic, and ExBody) has achieved remarkable results. However, these are trajectory-execution modules, not trajectory-generation modules. In settings where only sparse goals are provided, they depend on an external system to generate intermediate trajectories.

- Sparse and time-conditioned motion control:
Methods specifying only target states include Forward-Backward (FB) representations like BFM-Zero, BeJEPA, and keyframe-based PLAT. However, no prior method has combined accurate guidance in world coordinates, natural whole-body transitions, and pace adjustment suited to a requested arrival time.

- Motion in-betweening and controllable generation:
Generative models interpolating between keyframes using diffusion models (such as Kimodo and CondMDI) can produce kinematically plausible motions. However, when the generated trajectories are executed in closed loop on physics simulators or real robots, physical constraints such as torque limits and contacts mean there is no guarantee of reaching the accurate position on time.

S-BFM does not use generative models directly during inference; instead, it uses them during training as data augmentation to broaden the distances and durations the controller experiences, unifying all three requirements within a closed-loop physical controller.

sections.heading: The Three Learning Stages Powering S-BFM
sections.summary: S-BFM is trained across three stages: Spatial Grounding to embed world coordinates, Time-Conditioned Distillation to learn pacing from real data, and Generative Fine-Tuning to broaden coverage. At inference time, it operates without intermediate trajectories.
sections.details:
This section covers the problem formulation of S-BFM and its three-stage training pipeline.

### 3.1 Problem Formulation
A goal $g$ given to the robot comprises a planar position and heading (yaw), a target whole-body posture, and an arrival time $T$. It is defined in a fixed world frame $\mathcal{W}$ rooted at the robot's initial position. The controller continuously receives the remaining time $\Delta_t = T - t$, along with a mode flag $m$ indicating whether to hold that posture upon arrival (hold) or immediately transition to the next motion (continue).

### 3.2 Overview
The framework executes three training stages in sequence. Crucially, to prevent subsequent stages from degrading capabilities acquired in earlier stages, the state encoder $B_0$ and actor $\pi_0$ obtained in Stage I are completely frozen from Stage II onward, and the controller $C_\theta$ is trained on top of them.

### 3.3 Stage I: Spatial Grounding
The starting point is the Forward-Backward representation of BFM-Zero. Conventional latent spaces captured what posture the robot took, but did not maintain where it was located in world coordinates. To address this, root position and heading features $\rho_t$ are added to the encoder inputs and observation history. In addition, a readout decoder $H_\eta$ is introduced to recover root coordinates from latent embeddings, trained via a spatial reconstruction loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sp}}$. As a result, simply encoding a target state yields a latent code that directs the robot toward that location.

### 3.4 Stage II: Time-Conditioned Distillation
Stage I alone cannot determine how fast or along what path the robot should move. Therefore, actions from a teacher policy tracking dense reference trajectories are distilled into a student controller $C_\theta$ that observes only sparse goals and the normalized remaining time $\tau_t = \Delta_t / s_\tau$. By using DAgger-style closed-loop distillation where the student imitates the teacher along its own rollout trajectories, the student also acquires the ability to autonomously recover from intermediate drifts.

### 3.5 Stage III: Generative Fine-Tuning
In real-world motion capture data, specific posture transitions exist only for specific combinations of distances and durations (for example, standing-up motions always happen in place over the same number of seconds). To overcome this, a motion generator $\mathcal{G}_\omega$ distilled from a pre-trained diffusion model (Kimodo) is used to generate vast numbers of trajectories that synthetically vary distance $d$ and horizon $H$ for the same posture transition. By fine-tuning the controller on a mixture of real data and generated motions that pass physics checks, the model becomes robustly adaptable to unseen distances and extremely tight arrival times.

captions.F2: Detailed framework architecture. As shown in the bottom panel, with the encoder and actor from Stage I frozen, the controller $C_\theta$ is distilled in Stage II to output a time-conditioned latent code $\zeta_t$, and subsequently fine-tuned in Stage III using generated data.

sections.heading: Validation in Simulation and Real World: Striking Accuracy and Adaptability
sections.summary: Evaluated on a 29-DoF Unitree G1 in simulation and a full-size AGIBOT A3 robot. S-BFM cut global joint-position error by over 32% against baselines, exhibited high disturbance robustness, and demonstrated real-world gait switching between walking and running, as well as standing up.
sections.details:
Experiments were designed to answer four questions (Q1: sparse keyframe tracking, Q2: autonomous spatial goal reach and hold, Q3: stage-by-stage contributions, Q4: real-world performance).

### 4.1 Experimental Setup
Simulations utilized a 29-DoF Unitree G1 in MuJoCo (50 Hz control, 2 ms physics steps). Baselines included SONIC, UFO (UFO-FB), BeJEPA, and PLAT. Evaluation metrics covered joint-position error (MPJPE), root XY and yaw errors, on-time rate (OTR), target reach rate (Reach), and 5-second posture hold rate (Hold 5).

### 4.2 Sparse Keyframe Tracking (Q1)
Tracking performance was evaluated under both fixed and mixed horizon intervals. S-BFM demonstrated the best tracking accuracy in both settings, with global MPJPE of 38.35 cm and 37.60 cm, respectively. Notably, when intervals stretched to 2.5–3.5 s, baseline errors such as PLAT surged dramatically, whereas S-BFM maintained a flat error curve.

### 4.3 Spatial Goal Reach and Hold (Q2)
Over a 25-second evaluation horizon, robots were tested on reaching various postures (prone, sitting, crouching, single-leg stand) across distances from 0.4 to 4 m. Compared to BeJEPA, S-BFM boosted reach rate from 43.5% to 74.6%, increased Hold 5 from 7.4% to 35.2%, and cut terminal position error from 1.667 m down to 0.257 m. Under heavy lateral and downward torso disturbance impulses (1.5 / -1.0 m/s) at long distances of 3–4 m, BeJEPA reached only 23.6%, while S-BFM maintained high robustness with a 68.0% reach rate.

### 4.4 Ablation Studies (Q3)
With Stage I (P1) alone, the robot frequently dropped into a prone posture on the spot before moving toward the target location, rendering it immobilized (Figure F5). Adding Stage II (P2) enabled the proper transition sequence and pacing of approaching before dropping down, boosting on-time rate (OTR) from 4.63% to 17.35%. Incorporating Stage III (P3) dramatically raised the Hold 5 rate under short time horizons at 2 m from 13.6% to 92.0%.

### 4.5 Real-World Experiments (Q4)
Deployed on the full-size AGIBOT A3 humanoid, S-BFM achieved stable tracking across sparse instructions spaced 2 seconds apart and executed smooth continuous transitions across diverse postures. Furthermore, it autonomously adjusted its pacing—walking when given a 5-second horizon and running when given 3 seconds—and successfully executed whole-body coordination to stand up from a prone state on the floor.

captions.F4: Heatmap of reach rates across target distances (0.4 to 4 m) and disturbance conditions. Even in the challenging lower-right region with severe disturbances and longer distances, S-BFM maintains a high reach rate (68.0%), significantly outperforming the baseline (BeJEPA: 23.6%).
captions.F5: Simulation comparison across training stages. P1 alone collapses into a prone posture prematurely and fails to reach the target. As training progresses through P2 and P3, the robot runs toward the target location first and then naturally transitions into the prone posture.
captions.F6: Real-world experiments on the full-size AGIBOT A3 humanoid. (a) Stable tracking of sparse keyframes at 2-second intervals; (b) seamless whole-body transitions across different target postures.
captions.F7: Time adaptation and stand-up motion on the real robot. The robot autonomously switches its pace between walking for a 5-second horizon and running for 3 seconds to arrive on time, and also performs a natural stand-up motion from the floor.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Next Steps: Moving Toward End-to-End Training and VLA Integration
sections.summary: S-BFM shows that humanoids can autonomously organize whole-body motions from sparse spatiotemporal goals without intermediate trajectories. Future directions include unifying the three-stage training pipeline and interfacing with Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models.
sections.details:
This work demonstrates that humanoids can autonomously determine pacing and whole-body coordination from sparse spatiotemporal goals alone, eliminating the need for dense reference trajectories. Nonetheless, the authors outline three limitations and future directions:

- Complexity of the three-stage training pipeline:
Currently, spatial grounding, time distillation, and generative fine-tuning are conducted sequentially, raising the question of whether they can be unified into a single stage. Potential avenues include embedding remaining time and terminal conditions directly into Forward-Backward representations or Bellman updates, coupled with time-conditioned adversarial motion priors.

- Integration with Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and world models:
Interfaces allowing higher-level intelligent models like VLAs to output feasible, appropriate spatiotemporal goals remain unexplored. Tuning real-robot data collection workflows and high-level model objectives will be needed.

- Redesigning high-level architectures around S-BFM:
Because the low-level controller autonomously organizes intervening whole-body motions, high-level planners are relieved from frame-by-frame trajectory planning and can focus on scene understanding and task reasoning. Mechanisms where S-BFM feeds reachability feedback back to high-level models are also an exciting prospect.

takeaways: In whole-body humanoid control, explicitly providing a low-level controller with remaining time and world coordinates enables autonomous generation of natural pacing and transition motions without dense intermediate trajectories.
Freezing the encoder and actor from Forward-Backward representations and distilling a time-conditioned controller on top prevents catastrophic forgetting while building capabilities step-by-step.
For motion-duration combinations underrepresented in real data, kinematic generative models (diffusion models) serve as highly effective data augmentation to harden physical closed-loop controllers.
limitations: The three learning stages must be executed sequentially, making overall pipeline management and hyperparameter tuning complex.
The current implementation does not directly consume visual inputs such as camera imagery, leaving end-to-end integration with higher-level VLA models or environmental perception untested.
Only generated motions that pass physical filtering checks are utilized, making training efficiency sensitive to generative model quality and filtering criteria.
